summary: In Greek mythology, Ephialtes (Ancient Greek: Ἐφιάλτης) was one of the Giants (Gigantes), earthborn opponents of the Olympian gods in the Gigantomachy. Apollodorus says Apollo shot him in the left eye and Heracles in the right, blinding and killing him. Ancient art names him among the Giants fighting Zeus and other gods; mythographers treat him as distinct from the Aload of the same name.

sections.heading: Identity
paragraphs: Ephialtes appears in the catalogue of Giants who fought the Olympians. The Giants were, in the Hesiodic tradition, offspring of Gaia born from the blood of castrated Uranus. Later mythographers and vase painters give individual Giants names and opponents; Ephialtes is among those named both in Apollodorus and on Archaic Attic pottery.

Classical sources and modern scholarship distinguish this Gigante from Ephialtes of the Aloadae (Otus and Ephialtes), the Thessalian brothers who piled Pelion on Ossa. The shared name is noted already in discussions of the Gigantomachy tradition.

sections.heading: Mythology
paragraphs: According to Apollodorus (Bibliotheca 1.6.2), during the Gigantomachy Ephialtes was blinded by an arrow from Apollo in his left eye and by another arrow from Heracles in his right. Other Giants in the same narrative fall to Dionysus, Hecate, Hephaestus, and Athena, among others.

On early Attic black-figure vases Ephialtes is inscribed among Giants opposing Zeus (sometimes with Hyperbios and Agasthenes) and appears elsewhere fallen or engaged by Apollo; one early fifth-century red-figure column krater shows Poseidon attacking him. These images place him firmly in the Gigantomachy cycle rather than the Aload assault on Olympus.

sections.heading: Homonyms
paragraphs: This atlas entry (ephialtes-giant) is the earthborn Giant of the Gigantomachy. The Aload brother who piled mountains with Otus is tracked separately as ephialtes-aload.
